title: Object pronouns
objectives: I can tell a direct object from an indirect object and replace nouns with me, te, nos, o, a, os, as, lhe and lhes.
I can use everyday Brazilian patterns such as te amo, me liga, vi ele and short answers with no pronoun at all.
I can place pronouns correctly before the verb in speech, and recognize the hyphenated formal pattern in writing.
I can use pronouns after prepositions, including comigo, com você, para mim and para eu, and use dar with indirect pronouns.
I can explain why words such as dá, nós, ninguém and ajudá-lo are spelled and accented as they are.

vocabulary.note: Irregular. Present: eu dou, você dá, nós damos, eles dão. Preterite: dei, deu, demos, deram. The accent on dá marks a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, and keeps the verb apart from da, the unstressed de plus a. The person who receives is the indirect object: me deu, te deu.

example.target: Meu pai me deu este relógio.
example.source: My father gave me this watch.
example.source_literal: My father me gave this watch.

vocabulary.note: To borrow is pedir emprestado, literally to ask for lent. The person who receives the loan is the indirect object: me empresta. The em at the start is a nasal vowel, written with m because p follows.

example.target: Você pode me emprestar o carregador?
example.source: Can you lend me the charger?
example.source_literal: You can me to-lend the charger?

vocabulary.note: Also means to order someone to do something. The thing sent is the direct object and the receiver is the indirect object: me mandou uma mensagem.

example.target: Mandei uma mensagem para ela ontem.
example.source: I sent her a message yesterday.
example.source_literal: I-sent a message for her yesterday.

vocabulary.note: Takes a thing and a person: entregar o recibo ao cliente, or te entregar o recibo. The g is followed by a, so it is the hard g of go.

example.target: Vou entregar o pedido hoje à tarde.
example.source: I am going to deliver the order this afternoon.
example.source_literal: I-go to-deliver the order today at-the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Takes a thing and a person, like dar: devolvi o livro à biblioteca, or te devolvo tudo.

example.target: Preciso devolver o livro à biblioteca.
example.source: I need to return the book to the library.

vocabulary.note: Also means to turn on. The textbook pattern is ligar para alguém, but in speech the person is treated like a direct object: te ligo, me liga.

example.target: Vou te ligar mais tarde.
example.source: I will call you later.
example.source_literal: I-go you to-call more late.

vocabulary.note: To tell someone in advance, from a plain notice to a warning. Me avisa is the spoken command, which uses the ordinary present-tense form as in the imperative unit. Avisa has an s between two vowels, which is said z.

example.target: Me avisa se você vai atrasar.
example.source: Let me know if you are going to be late.
example.source_literal: Me warn if you go to-be-late.

vocabulary.note: Also means to count numbers. The same verb covers counting and recounting a story, as in English recount. The thing told is the direct object and the listener is the indirect object: me conta. Incrível has an accent because of its stress; see the spelling note.

example.target: Ele me contou uma novidade incrível.
example.source: He told me some incredible news.
example.source_literal: He me counted a novelty incredible.

vocabulary.note: To ask a question; to ask for something is pedir. The person asked is an indirect object: perguntei a ele, me perguntou. The gu stays a real u sound here (per-gun-TAR) because gu only hides its u before e or i.

example.target: Vou perguntar para ela onde fica o banco.
example.source: I will ask her where the bank is.
example.source_literal: I-go to-ask to her where stays the bank.

vocabulary.note: The person answered is an indirect object: ele me respondeu, respondi a ele. A word-initial r is the strong r, like a breathy English h.

example.target: Ela ainda não me respondeu.
example.source: She has not answered me yet.
example.source_literal: She still not me answered.

vocabulary.note: The person invited is a direct object (te convido, convidei ele); the event follows with para.

example.target: Vou convidar vocês para o meu aniversário.
example.source: I am going to invite you all to my birthday.
example.source_literal: I-go to-invite you-all for the my birthday.

vocabulary.note: The person introduced is the direct object and the person they meet is the indirect object: apresentei ele à minha mãe. A single s between vowels is said z.

example.target: Posso te apresentar a minha amiga?
example.source: May I introduce you to my friend?
example.source_literal: Can-I you to-introduce the my friend?

vocabulary.note: The person thanked is an indirect object: agradeço a você, or te agradeço. The thing is introduced with por: pela ajuda is por plus a plus ajuda. The ce is said se, and the ç of agradeço writes the s sound before o (see the spelling note).

example.target: Quero agradecer a vocês pela ajuda.
example.source: I want to thank you all for the help.
example.source_literal: I-want to-thank to you-all for-the help.

vocabulary.note: The skill is the thing taught and the pupil is the indirect object: me ensinou. A verb that follows takes the linking preposition a. The en is a nasal vowel, and the nh of cozinhar is the ny of canyon.

example.target: Minha tia me ensinou a cozinhar.
example.source: My aunt taught me to cook.
example.source_literal: My aunt me taught to to-cook.

vocabulary.note: Te amo is warm and strong: it is said to partners, children, parents and very close friends. Gostar de is the weaker verb for liking.

example.target: Eu te amo muito.
example.source: I love you very much.
example.source_literal: I you love much.

vocabulary.note: The preposition em is part of the verb, so the person is never me or te directly: confio em você. Em joins the pronoun: em plus ele is nele.

example.target: Eu confio em você.
example.source: I trust you.
example.source_literal: I trust in you.

vocabulary.note: Also estar com saudade de, literally to be with longing of. Saudade is a noun for the ache of being away from a person, place or time; English has no single word for it. The preposition de stays, so the pronoun is you, not te. In saudade the au is one diphthong, and d before an i sound is said j as in judge.

example.target: Sinto saudade de você.
example.source: I miss you.
example.source_literal: I-feel longing of you.

vocabulary.note: Also means the present (time); context decides. The single s between vowels is said z.

example.target: Comprei um presente para você.
example.source: I bought a gift for you.

vocabulary.note: Built from novo, new, and singular in Portuguese: uma novidade is one piece of news. The ending -dade matches English -ty, as in cidade and universidade.

example.target: Tenho uma novidade para te contar.
example.source: I have some news to tell you.
example.source_literal: I-have a novelty for you to-tell.

vocabulary.note: The money handed back after you pay. It belongs to the family of trocar, to exchange, which appears in the first dialogue.

example.target: O caixa me deu o troco errado.
example.source: The cashier gave me the wrong change.
example.source_literal: The cashier me gave the change wrong.

vocabulary.note: Nota fiscal is the official tax receipt or invoice. The ci is said si.

example.target: Pode me dar o recibo, por favor?
example.source: Can you give me the receipt, please?
example.source_literal: Can-you me give the receipt, please?

vocabulary.note: An order sent to you or made for you. The en is a nasal vowel, written with n because the next letter is c, not p or b.

example.target: A encomenda chegou hoje de manhã.
example.source: The parcel arrived this morning.
example.source_literal: The parcel arrived today of morning.

grammar.title: Direct and indirect objects: who receives what
grammar.explanation:
Every action has a subject, the one who acts, and often an object, the person or thing the action reaches (the grammar map lesson introduced both terms). Grammar sorts objects into two kinds, and this whole unit depends on the difference. A direct object receives the action itself, with no preposition between it and the verb. To find it, ask the verb "whom or what?": in "Ana sees Pedro", Pedro answers whom. An indirect object is the person who benefits from the action, receives something, or is addressed, and Portuguese joins it to the verb with the preposition a or para. To find it, ask "to whom or for whom?". One verb can have both: in "Ana gives Pedro the book", the book is the direct object (what is given) and Pedro is the indirect object (who receives it).

English hides the difference in two ways. First, it can drop the preposition and rely on word order: "I gave her the book" and "I gave the book to her" mean the same thing, and in the first version nothing marks "her" as indirect. Second, English pronouns do not change with the role: "her" is the same word in "I saw her" (direct) and "I gave her a book" (indirect). Portuguese keeps the preposition visible: Eu dei o livro à Ana, where à is a plus a, the crase from the places unit. And in the third person Portuguese pronouns do mark the two roles, as the next note shows. So the first skill of this unit is to ask "whom or what?" versus "to whom?" and to notice which answer the Portuguese verb expects.

The second skill is to accept that the Portuguese verb, not the English translation, decides the role. Some verbs take an indirect object where English uses a direct one. Responder (to answer) is literally to answer to someone: respondi à Ana, "I answered to Ana". Perguntar (to ask), agradecer (to thank) and telefonar (to phone) work the same way. Other verbs take a direct object, like ver (to see), convidar (to invite) and amar (to love). A third group carries a fixed preposition that never disappears: confiar em (literally to trust in), gostar de (to like, literally to like of) and sentir saudade de (to miss, literally to feel longing of). Verbs of this third group never take me or te directly. The preposition stays and the pronoun changes to its form after a preposition: confio em você, gosto de você, sinto saudade de você.

In everyday speech the boundary blurs: Brazilians say Ela me ligou, treating the person as a direct object, although the textbook form is ligar para alguém. This costs nothing in the first and second person, because me, nos and te are the same word in both roles. The classification matters most in the third person and in writing, which is where the next note turns.

grammar.title: The pronoun forms: me, te, nos, o, a, lhe and what Brazilians say instead
grammar.explanation:
A pronoun replaces a noun so that you need not repeat it, and an object pronoun replaces the object: "Ana gave Pedro the book" becomes "She gave him it". Portuguese object pronouns are clitics, as the reflexive lesson explained: short unstressed words that lean on the verb and are said as one word with it, so Eu te amo is pronounced eu-chi-A-mu. English also changes the pronoun between subject and object (I becomes me, he becomes him), but Portuguese separates more: in the third person it has different forms for the direct and the indirect object.

First and second person. Me (me, to me) and nos (us, to us) work as direct and indirect objects alike, so Ela me viu (she saw me) and Ela me deu um livro (she gave me a book) use the same word. For "you", everyday speech uses te in both roles. This looks inconsistent, because você is grammatically third person: the subject pronouns lesson showed that it began as a noun phrase. Brazilians nevertheless pair você with te, as in Você sabe que eu te adoro. Te is originally the object form of tu, and speakers of você adopted it. The grammatically consistent choices for você, o, a and lhe, survive mainly in writing and in formal service language.

Third person. The written system has four direct forms: o (him, it), a (her, it), os (them, masculine or mixed) and as (them, feminine). They agree in gender and number with what they replace, so Vi o Pedro becomes Eu o vi and Comprei as flores becomes Eu as comprei. For the indirect role there are lhe (to him, to her, to you) and lhes (to them, to you all), which do not show gender: Dei o livro ao Pedro becomes Eu lhe dei o livro. These forms are correct, and standard in writing, in speeches and in polite service language. In ordinary conversation they are mostly replaced.

The table has a written system on the left and an everyday system on the right. The everyday system is simpler. Me and te do not change. For the third person it uses ele, ela, eles and elas directly after the verb as the direct object, and para or pra plus the same word as the indirect object. For "us" it often uses a gente. Learn the written forms to read and write, and the everyday forms to speak.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the pronouns and the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This note applies the rules of the sound and accent lessons to the new words of this unit, so that no spelling is left unexplained. Start with the pronouns, which are unstressed words, so the weak-vowel rule applies: a final unstressed e is said i and a final unstressed o is said u. Me is therefore mi, te is chi (t before an i sound becomes the ch of "cheese", as in the reflexive lesson), o is u and os is us. Nos is nus, and the accent is what separates it from a different word: nós (we) is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a vowel plus s, which the stress lesson says takes an accent, while nos (us) is unstressed and takes none. Lhe and lhes begin with the digraph lh, the sound of "lli" in "million", so lhe is said lyi: the lh, then the weak final e as i.

After a preposition the forms are mim and ti. Mim is said mĩ: the final m after a vowel is not a consonant but the sign that the i is nasal, as in sim. Ti is said chi, like te. The fused forms follow the same logic. In comigo the g is followed by o, so it is the hard g of "go", and the word is co-MI-gu. In contigo the n before t marks a nasal o and t before i is ch: con-CHI-gu. In conosco the n starts the second syllable, so the first o is a plain oral vowel. Here sc before o is not the single sound it has before e (nascer): the s and the hard c are both said, as in "scar", giving co-NOS-ku.

In formal writing, o and a attach to the verb with a hyphen, and the attachment changes the spelling. Take comprar plus o. The written form drops the final r and attaches lo (an old sound change in which the r, s or z of the verb merged with the pronoun): comprá-lo. Without the r, the verb form comprá is stressed on its last syllable and ends in a, where the default is the second to last, so by the stress lesson it must carry an accent. The vowel is an open a, so the accent is acute. In the same way fazer plus o gives fazê-lo (the e of fazer is closed, so the mark is a circumflex) and ajudar plus o gives ajudá-lo. After a nasal ending, the pronoun becomes no or na and the verb does not change: compraram plus o gives compraram-no.

The table explains, with the same four-step procedure (divide into syllables, find the stress, read the default from the ending, compare), every other spelling in this unit that was not explained before. Three families recur in it. The accents on você, dá, relógio, ninguém and difícil are all the same event: the stressed syllable differs from what the ending predicts, so the stressed vowel is marked, and open or closed quality picks acute or circumflex. The tilde words (amanhã, então, estão, mãe) mark a nasal vowel, and because ã and ão already default to the last syllable, the tilde needs no companion. And every consonant letter that looks odd (ç, qu, gu, ch, nh, lh, x, s between vowels) is a fixed convention from the sounds lesson; none of them is irregular.

rows: A stressed one-syllable word ending in a or o takes an accent. In dá it also separates the verb from the unstressed da, which is de plus a. Tá is está with its first syllable dropped in speech.
The tilde marks a nasal vowel, and ão by default is stressed on the last syllable, so no accent is needed.
Stressed on the last syllable, but the ending em defaults to the second to last, so the stressed vowel takes an accent, as in também.
The final io counts as two vowels, so the stress falls on the third to last syllable, which always takes an accent. The vowel is open, so the mark is acute. The g before i is zh.
Stressed on the second to last syllable, but the ending l defaults to the last, so an accent is required. The vowel i has one quality, so the mark is acute. Final l is said w.
A single s between two vowels is said z.
Double s writes the s sound between vowels, which a single s would make z.
c before e or i is said s.
x after ai is said sh.
g before e and j are said zh. The h of hoje is silent. Final em is a nasal glide.
nh is the ny of canyon. The ending ã is stressed by default, so no accent is needed.
au is a diphthong, one beat. d before an i sound is said j as in judge, and final e is said i.
Word-initial r and rr are the strong r, like a breathy English h. ch is sh. sc before o is s then k.
em or en before a consonant marks a nasal vowel: m before p, n elsewhere. It is not pronounced as a consonant.
c would say k before a, o or u, so the cedilla ç writes the s sound there. It never starts a word and never appears before e or i. In almoço the l closes a syllable, so it is said w.

The tilde marks a nasal vowel. ã and ão default to a stressed last syllable, so the tilde alone is enough and no acute is added. Mãe is one syllable, the diphthong ãe. In decisão the s between vowels is z and the ci is si.
a-ma-NYAH, mãy, ĩ-TOW, es-TOW, de-si-ZOW (nasal, ow as in now)

Stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so the accent is always written. In Júlia the final ia counts as two vowels for this rule. The vowel is open a, and u takes only the acute.

Você and vocês are stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for e and es, and the closed e takes the circumflex. É is a stressed one-syllable word with an open e, which separates is from the unstressed e, and. À records the fusion of the preposition a and the article a.
Qu before e or i is k and the u is silent. Gu keeps a real u sound before a, o or a consonant; the u is silent only before e or i.

grammar.title: The everyday Brazilian system: vi ele, te amo and dropped objects
grammar.explanation:
The written system of the previous notes is what grammar books teach, and every Brazilian can read and write it. Spoken Brazilian Portuguese has simplified it. The third-person direct forms o, a, os and as have nearly disappeared from conversation, and lhe and lhes sound formal. Textbooks call parts of what replaced them non-standard, but it is the ordinary spoken grammar of educated Brazilians, and you can use it with confidence.

Replacement one: ele, ela, eles and elas directly after the verb. Eu vi ele, Eu convidei elas, Eu conheço eles. English changes the pronoun between subject and object (he becomes him), so "I saw he" sounds like a mistake to an English ear. In Portuguese, ele and ela are one word in both roles, the way "you" is in English ("you see me", "I see you"), and in speech Brazilians treat them that way. Keep this for people. For an indirect object the replacement is para or pra plus the same word: Dei o livro pra ele.

Replacement two: te for every "you", and a gente for "us". Posso te ajudar? and Vou te ligar are the norm with everyone, even strangers addressed as você. A gente literally means "the people" (it began as a noun) and means "we": Ele viu a gente, Ele chamou a gente. Nos survives in writing and in fixed phrases.

Replacement three: no pronoun at all. When the object is a thing and the context is clear, Brazilians leave it out. Você comprou o pão? is answered Comprei, not Comprei-o and not Comprei ele. English cannot do this: "I bought" alone is incomplete, so English must say "I bought it". Portuguese lets the verb stand alone, because its ending already says who acted and the question has supplied what. The same works for short answers: Você viu o filme? Vi, sim. Or the speaker repeats the noun. This is why o and a are rare in speech: what they did for things is done by silence or repetition, and what they did for people is done by ele and ela.

Formal contexts still use the written forms: Posso ajudá-lo? or Posso ajudar o senhor? (to a man), Enviamos-lhe o documento in a formal email. They add politeness and you should be able to read them, but they are not needed in ordinary speech. Moving between registers is normal: a Brazilian writes Te ligo to a friend and Enviamos-lhe o documento in a business letter.

grammar.title: Where the pronoun goes: before the verb in speech, after it in formal writing
grammar.explanation:
A clitic pronoun has no stress of its own, so it must lean on a verb, and the question is on which side. Textbook grammar, and the Portuguese of Portugal, usually puts it after the verb, joined by a hyphen (enclisis): Diga-me, Deu-me a chave. Brazilian speech almost always puts it before the verb (proclisis): Me diz, Ela me deu a chave. The reflexive lesson used the same two terms, and the preference is the same. For speaking, the rule is short: put the pronoun directly before its verb and never worry about it.

Formal writing adds one restriction: a sentence should not open with a clitic pronoun. A sentence that begins with the verb therefore puts the pronoun after it, with a hyphen: Diga-me a verdade, Avisaram-nos. As soon as something stands before the verb, the pronoun goes in front of it even in writing: a subject (Ela me disse tudo), a negative word (Não te vi ontem, Ninguém me avisou), a question word, or que (Eu sei que você me ama). In speech, Me diz a verdade is natural even at the start of a sentence.

When two verbs appear together, Brazilians attach the pronoun to the verb it belongs to in meaning, which is the infinitive, and put it in front of that verb: Vou te ligar, Posso te ajudar?, Quero te contar uma coisa. The pronoun is the object of ligar, ajudar and contar, not of vou, posso or quero. The hyphen pattern Vou ligar-te is grammatical in writing, but it sounds stiff in Brazil.

The hyphenated written forms change spelling, and the previous spelling note explains why. Me, te, lhe, nos and lhes attach unchanged: Diga-me, Deu-lhe. The pronouns o and a become lo and la after a verb ending in r, s or z, which lose that letter (comprá-lo, fazê-lo), and no and na after a nasal ending (compraram-no).

grammar.title: After prepositions: mim, ti, comigo, the subject of an infinitive, and dar
grammar.explanation:
Clitic pronouns lean on verbs. After a preposition there is no verb to lean on, so Portuguese uses a different set, the stressed pronouns, which can carry emphasis and stand alone. English uses one set for both jobs ("me" in "see me" and in "for me"), so this is a real second system. Two forms are special: mim for eu and ti for tu. Every other form is the subject pronoun unchanged: para você, para ele, para ela, para nós, para a gente, para vocês. Contractions from earlier still apply: dele, nela.

With com, the first and second person fuse into single words: comigo (with me), contigo (with you, only for tu) and conosco (with us, formal or written); consigo means with himself, herself or themselves. The odd shape has a reason. In Latin the preposition came after the pronoun (mecum, "with me"), and when the word stopped being understood that way, com was added in front again, so com appears twice. In everyday Brazilian speech comigo is universal, but com você and com a gente are far more common than contigo and conosco. After entre (between), the standard form is mim: Isso fica entre mim e você.

One classic trap. When the pronoun is the subject of a following infinitive, use the subject form eu, not mim. In É difícil para eu entender, the person who understands is eu, so the subject pronoun is required, even though a preposition precedes it. The infinitive itself does not change for eu; the pronoun in front of it shows who the subject is. English speakers go wrong because English says "for me to understand" with the object form "me". The test is whether a verb follows: Isso é para mim has no verb after it, so mim. Esse livro é para eu ler has the verb ler, so eu. The same logic explains Deixa eu ver (let me see), where eu is the subject of ver.

Finally, dar (to give) is the model verb for two objects. The present is eu dou, você dá, nós damos, eles dão, and the preterite dei, deu, demos, deram. The thing given is the direct object and the receiver is the indirect object: Me dá um minuto, Ele te deu o troco? For a third-person receiver, speech prefers para or pra plus ele or ela: Dei o presente pra ela. Lhe belongs to formal writing: Dei-lhe o livro. The spoken idiom dá pra plus infinitive, "it is possible to", comes from the same verb: literally it gives for.

culture.title: Te amo, me liga and the gap between writing and speech
culture.text:
Brazilian Portuguese has an unusually wide gap between what grammar books prescribe and what people say. Eu vi ele, me liga and te amo are heard everywhere, from television to the university, while eu o vi, ligue-me and amo-te sound stiff or belong to Portugal. Brazilians handle the gap easily: they write a formal email or a contract with lhe and the hyphen, and they talk to friends with me and te. A learner who speaks the everyday pattern will be understood and sounds natural, while someone who speaks in textbook forms may sound like a letter.

The pronoun te is the great connector. Even when you address a stranger as você, it is normal to say posso te ajudar? or vou te mandar o endereço. In parts of the South, the North and the Northeast, speakers also use tu, with contigo and ti. Messages between friends are full of these patterns: me avisa quando chegar, te ligo depois and me manda uma foto. The word saudade appears constantly in them, as in Tô com saudade de você. Tô is the spoken short form of estou, with the first syllable dropped, and it keeps its circumflex because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in o. The whole phrase literally says I am with longing of you, and it is a very warm way to tell someone you miss them.
